owner.occupation: Live sound engineer at club venues

world.bio: Twenty years mixing loud rooms on Red River Street: Mohawk, Emo's, a couple of venues that don't exist anymore. Started as a stagehand at nineteen, learned on a Soundcraft board somebody left in a closet. Tinnitus showed up four years ago after a punk festival and never left. I coach Little League, restore a 1970s Honda CB, and have recently become strangely obsessed with how good a quiet mix can sound.
skills_assets: Twenty years of live sound at club and small-theatre scale (200 to 1,500 capacity)
Ears that now work from experience rather than from raw hearing
A rig of two small-format digital consoles and a pair of line-array speakers
SPL meters, calibrated, and a spreadsheet of room measurements for six venues
Contacts with about thirty touring and local bands
A garage shop with a 1974 Honda CB550 half rebuilt

projects.name: Quiet mixes
projects.text: Got tinnitus a few years ago and now spends his spare time designing mixes that sound full under 70 dB. I record a local trio in my garage with the ceiling cut to 68 dB and treat the low end by hand, swapping out kick drum for a soft felt beater, rolling off harshness above 8 kHz. It's strange: the fullness comes from the mids, not the loudness. I'm keeping notes on EQ curves for each instrument at low SPL.

projects.name: CB550 restoration
projects.text: 1974 Honda, bought for $800, bones are good. New carburettor kit, wiring harness and tank paint remain. It sits next to the workbench like a patient.

projects.name: Little League
projects.text: Coaching an 8-and-under team, 11 kids, 4 wins 6 losses. Mostly we're teaching them not to cry when they miss.

notes.text: Mixed a band at Mohawk, 101 dB at the board. Wore my earplugs and still came home with a ringing so loud I could hear it over the fridge. Lay on the couch and listened to the tone, it's a G-sharp today, almost.

Garage experiment: trio recording at 68 dB. Acoustic guitar, upright bass, brushes on a snare. When the room is quiet, you hear the wood in the bass. I'd never noticed it at 100 dB. It was always there, I couldn't hear it.
Little League game. We lost 12 to 3. One kid hit the ball twice and cried both times. Told him that's two more than last week. He smiled.

Moved mom into assisted living on Monday. She took her afghan and the radio. Asked me to set the station to the oldies. She said, 'It's nice, but it's quiet.' I thought: yes, ma'am, I'm working on that.
Messed up the CB carb kit, one float needle wrong, got gas all over the floor. Spent two hours cleaning, then sat on the motorcycle and just held the handlebars.

Read an article on sensory-friendly concerts for kids. The suggested level was 70 dB or below, no strobing, quiet space. I thought, that's what I've been doing in the garage for a year, but nobody asked for it.
Audiologist said the tinnitus is stable. 'Stable' is a word that means 'not getting worse yet'. I asked about hearing aids. She said not yet. I said fine and drove home with the radio off.

Quiet gig idea: a show for people who can't handle loud rooms. Kids, folks with sensitivities, old-timers like my mom. I don't know who'd put it on or where. Wrote it on the whiteboard in the garage and left it.
Little League, our first win. 9 to 7. The kids dumped a cooler of lukewarm Gatorade on me. I was soaked for the rest of the afternoon and I didn't care.

messages.text: Leader: Great mix tonight. Dale: Thanks. Leader: A little hot on the vocals though. Dale: That's the room. Leader: You and the room, man.
Ray: How's Mom doing? Dale: Okay. She misses the house. Ray: I can come down on the 25th. Dale: Please. She likes it when you visit.
Bassist: You really want me to play that soft? Dale: Try it. Bassist: Feels weird. Dale: Listen to the recording. Bassist: Okay, that's actually nice.
Office: Your next appointment is January 12. Dale: Can I come earlier? Office: Is it urgent? Dale: Not really. Office: Then January 12.
Parent: Thanks for coaching. Dale: Thanks for bringing the snacks. Parent: My boy says you're the nicest coach. Dale: He's the loudest hitter.

relations.about: 79, moved into assisted living, misses radio and her garden.
Lives in San Antonio, helps with Mom.
Local acoustic band; the bassist is the friendliest.

constraints: Cannot work shows over 95 dB without breaks
Evenings are for Little League and venue gigs, mornings are free
Will only work on projects that treat sound with care
Budget for gear is limited to about $1,500
sensitive: Tinnitus is bad some nights and he sometimes cries about it
Worries he'll lose hearing and therefore lose his career
Money is thin; he's paying for his mom's assisted living partly
